tip: The suffix '-yla' means with: 'başarısıyla' means with her success, one word doing the job of a preposition.
To say despite, use '-masına rağmen': 'yağmasına rağmen' means despite the fact that it rained.
'içmek' is to drink; add '-ir' and it means make someone drink, so 'içirdik' is we made someone drink.
'buyurun' is an all-purpose polite word for go ahead or help yourself. 'içeri buyurun' means please come in.
'kendi başıma' is a set phrase for on my own, by myself. Change 'başıma' to 'başına' for on your own.
The '-ır' ending on 'toplanır' marks a routine, not a one-off: trash gets collected regularly, every morning.
The '-malı' in 'okumalıyız' marks necessity: we should read. Add '-malı' or '-meli' to any verb for must or should.
The '-ınca' on 'çıkınca' means when or as soon as. It attaches to the verb, so Turkish needs no separate word for when.
'buçuk' means and a half after a number: 'iki buçuk saat' is two and a half hours.
The '-muştu' on 'doğmuştu' is the past perfect: the sun had already risen before another past moment.
In a passive sentence, 'tarafından' marks the doer: 'polis tarafından yakalandı' is was caught by the police.
'başınız sağ olsun' is the set condolence phrase, literally may your head stay well. Used only to offer sympathy.
'bulsun' (let him find) plus 'diye' means so that: 'bulsun diye bekledik' is we waited so that he would find one.
The '-seydim' in 'etseydim' marks an unreal if: 'şarj etseydim' means if I had charged it, implying I did not.
To fast is 'oruç tutmak', literally to hold a fast. Turkish pairs 'oruç' with 'tutmak', hold, not a single verb.
'yürü-' means walk; adding '-t' makes it made someone walk, so 'yürüttü' is she made me walk. Add '-t' or '-dır' to say you made someone do it.
'-ınca' means when or once: 'ısın-' (warm up) plus '-ınca' gives 'ısınınca', once it warmed up. No separate word for when is needed.
For how often, the time unit takes '-da': 'haftada iki kez' means twice a week, with '-da' carrying the sense of per.
'içinde' after a time span means within: 'yirmi dakika içinde' is within twenty minutes. The noun before it stays plain, no case ending.
'kimse' (nobody) needs a negative verb: 'kimse gelmedi' means nobody came. Turkish doubles the negative, 'kimse' plus '-me' on the verb.
'beğenmek' (to like) takes a marked object: 'ayakkabıları çok beğendim', I really liked the shoes, marked by '-ı' on 'ayakkabıları'.
Turning toward something uses '-a/-e': 'sol' (left) becomes 'sola' in 'sola dönün', turn to the left.
'pek' before a negative means not really: 'pek beğenmedi' is didn't really like it. 'pek' needs the negative verb to carry this sense.
'yoksa' joins two choices in a question as or: 'yeter mi, yoksa daha fazla mı' is it enough or is more needed. Each choice keeps its 'mı'.
When you have someone do a job, the doer takes '-a/-e': 'boyacıya' with 'boyattık' means we had the painter paint it for us.
'Sayın' before a name or title is a formal Dear or Esteemed: 'Sayın müdürüm' opens a polite or written address to a director.
'önce' ... 'sonra' frames a sequence as first ... then: 'önce soğanları doğrarsın, sonra kavurursun', first you chop, then you fry.
For age, add '-ında' to 'yaş': 'seksen yaşında' means eighty years old, literally at the age of eighty.
After a number the noun stays singular: 'üç kilo domates', three kilos of tomato, never 'domatesler'. No plural '-ler' follows a count.
'-se de' on a verb means even though: 'gitse de' means even though she goes, though she goes there regularly.
